text: Five lessons, five tools. This lesson doesn't add a sixth — it's the decision framework that turns "I know what each tool does" into "I know which one to reach for." That's both what the exam tests and what actually matters when a stakeholder describes a requirement in plain English.

Walk it in order. Does it only need to stop a bad save? Validation rule. Does it only display a calculated value, never store it? Formula field. Does it need a stored aggregate from direct children? Roll-up summary. Does it need named humans to sign off with an audit trail? Approval process. Does it branch, loop, need a screen, or touch several objects? Flow. And if it still doesn't fit after all five — bulk, transactional, algorithmically complex — that's Apex.

Two requirements can sound almost identical. "Require a reason when an opportunity is closed lost" — one condition, no side effect, validation rule. "When an opportunity is closed lost, notify the sales manager and log a task" — same trigger, but now there's a side effect. That's an action, not a block. That's Flow. Same surface language, different answer, because what changed is whether it blocks or acts.

A few quick ones. Blocking a case with no description — validation rule. Showing days since created — formula field. Total open opportunity value on an account — roll-up summary. Director sign-off before a large contract activates — approval process. Auto-assigning a lead by territory and workload — Flow. A nightly batch recalculating loyalty tiers for two hundred thousand customers — that's Apex territory.

Real apps rarely use exactly one tool. A roll-up summary might feed a validation rule's threshold. A Flow might evaluate conditions and then call Submit for Approval. A formula field might compute the value a validation rule checks. The actual skill isn't finding one tool that does everything — it's choosing the right tool per requirement and letting them compose.

Block, calculate, aggregate, route, branch, and only then code — that's the path. Chapter four picks up from here: how a finished application actually gets delivered, reported on, secured, deployed, and adopted.
